screens.title: Enums and Records (Java 16+)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will explore two language features that make Java code clearer and safer: enums and records. Enums give you a typed set of named constants that can carry fields, constructors, and methods so each constant can behave like a small object. Records, introduced as a standard feature in Java 16, let you declare immutable data carriers without boilerplate for constructors, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString. You will see practical examples: a traffic light enum with actions and durations, and a book record that shows how records auto-generate accessors and equality. As you learn, notice common pitfalls: using enums for values that change, or assuming records are mutable like POJOs. We’ll also practice by building a Currency enum and a Transaction record to illustrate how these features combine in a realistic application. By the end you will understand when an enum improves type safety and when a record reduces boilerplate, and you’ll be able to pick the right tool for representing fixed choices or simple immutable data.

screens.title: Why choose enums over static constants?
screens.narratorSegment: Before enums, Java code commonly used public static final integers or strings to name fixed values. That pattern allows invalid assignments, loses semantic type information, and requires the reader to know the valid range by convention. An enum is a special class representing a fixed set of instances; it prevents invalid values at compile time because the type itself limits possible assignments. Enums also permit fields, methods, and constructors so each constant can bundle data and behavior. For example, if you model traffic lights, a plain integer gives you no direct place for the action text or duration. Using an enum you can store both and call methods like getDuration. A common misconception is that enums are only simple labels; in fact they are full-featured types and can implement interfaces, be used in switch statements, and be iterated. Use enums when the set of allowed values is closed and meaningful in the domain. When values are open-ended or configuration-driven, prefer classes or other structures. Consider refactoring groups of related static finals into enums to increase safety and clarity. Why choose enums over static constants? means enums make sets of fixed choices type-safe and expressive by allowing per-constant data and methods.. In practical terms, type safety, readability, and behavioral constants. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Enums vs static constants
Problem with static constants
Using public static final ints or strings does not restrict valid values and encourages scattered constants. It is easy to accidentally pass invalid values or mix constants from different contexts.
  • • No compile-time restriction on allowed values.
  • • Harder to attach per-value data or behavior.
  • • Readability suffers when many constants exist.
Example
Replace grouped static constants with an enum to improve safety and attach behavior.
Benefits of enums
Enums are classes: each constant is an instance and can hold fields, constructors, and methods. The compiler enforces valid assignments and you can iterate values or use them in switches for clear logic.
Key capabilities:
  • • Type safety: only enum values are allowed.
  • • Expressive: per-constant data and methods.
  • • Iteration and switch support for clear control flow.
Misconception
Enums are not limited to simple labels; they are full classes and can implement interfaces.

screens.title: Enum syntax and semantics
screens.narratorSegment: An enum declaration defines a special class whose constants are predefined instances. Each constant you list at the top is created by calling the enum’s constructor. Enum constructors are implicitly private, which prevents external code from creating new instances. You can add fields that all constants hold, initialize them via the constructor, and expose behavior through methods. For example the TrafficLightColor enum attaches an action string and duration in seconds to each color. Iterating over TrafficLightColor. values() returns every defined constant, and calling methods on each constant accesses its associated data. A common error is trying to mark the enum constructor as public; the correct pattern is private or package-private. Another mistake is using enums for values that are not fixed — choose enums only when the domain set truly is closed. Understanding that each constant is a typed instance helps you design richer domain models while keeping compile-time safety. Enum syntax and semantics means constants are instances; constructors initialize per-constant fields; methods provide behavior per constant.. In practical terms, how an enum becomes a set of instances with fields and methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Enum Syntax
TrafficLightColor example
public enum TrafficLightColor {
    RED("Stop", 60),
    YELLOW("Prepare to stop", 5),
    GREEN("Go", 45);

    private final String action;
    private final int durationSeconds;

    TrafficLightColor(String action, int durationSeconds) {
      this.action = action;
      this.durationSeconds = durationSeconds;
    }

    public String getAction() { return action; }
    public int getDurationSeconds() { return durationSeconds; }

    public void displayInfo() {
      System.out.println("Color: " + this.name() + ", Action: " + action + ", Duration: " + durationSeconds + "s");
    }
}
Walkthrough
  • • Enum constants RED, YELLOW, GREEN call the enum constructor with parameters.
  • • Fields action and durationSeconds store per-constant data and are final.
  • • The constructor is not public; enum instances are created only by the enum itself.
  • • Methods like getAction or displayInfo operate on the current instance.
Common mistake
Do not declare enum constructors public. Enums control their instance creation.

screens.title: Iterating and switching on enums
screens.narratorSegment: Working with enums in control flow is straightforward and safer than numeric constants. You can iterate through all constants with the values() method and inspect each constant’s name or data. The name method returns the declared identifier, and you can use getters to access attached fields. Enums also integrate with switch statements to produce clear, type-checked branches. Because the switch parameter must be an enum type, the compiler helps you notice missing branches when you enable warnings. A common pattern is iterating and printing or performing actions per constant in a loop. For example, for a traffic simulation you might loop through TrafficLightColor. values() and call displayInfo on each constant. A common misconception is that an enum’s name can be changed at runtime — it cannot. If you need dynamically configured choices you should not use an enum. Using enums in switches and iterations leads to more maintainable code and reduces runtime mistakes that arise from incorrect string or integer comparisons. Iterating and switching on enums means use values() to iterate and enum-typed switches for clear, compiler-checked control flow.. In practical terms, using values(), name(), and switch safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Iterate & Switch
Iteration example
for (TrafficLightColor c : TrafficLightColor.values()) {
    System.out.println(c.name() + " → " + c.getAction());

Switch example
switch (currentColor) {

    // stop
    break;
  case YELLOW:
    // slow down
    break;
  case GREEN:
    // go

Using switch with enum types gives you clear branches and avoids invalid case values. Iteration and name access let you build user lists and diagnostics easily.

screens.title: Introduction to Records
screens.narratorSegment: Records provide a compact way to declare a class whose primary purpose is to carry immutable data. When you declare a record with a list of components, the compiler generates a canonical constructor, accessor methods named after each component, equals and hashCode implementations based on all components, and a toString that lists the components. The components are final, which makes records immutable by design. Records reduce boilerplate dramatically compared to traditional POJOs where you must write fields, constructors, getters, and override equality methods. A helpful comparison is a Book implemented as a long POJO versus a Book record: the record declaration is a single line and already includes correct equality semantics. Records can still include custom methods and static members, but they cannot declare additional instance fields beyond the components, nor can they extend other classes. This design keeps records focused and predictable as data carriers. Introduction to Records means records are immutable data carriers that auto-generate constructor, accessors, equals, hashcode, and tostring.. In practical terms, concise immutable data classes in java 16 and later. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Records
POJO vs Record (boilerplate)
// Traditional POJO
class OldBook {
  private final String title;
  private final String author;
  private final int yearPublished;
  public OldBook(String title, String author, int y) { ... }
  public String getTitle() { return title; }
  // equals(), hashCode(), toString() boilerplate omitted
}

// Record (Java 16+)
record Book(String title, String author, int yearPublished) { }
Record features
  • • Canonical constructor is generated for all components.
  • • Accessors are named after components, e.g., title().
  • • equals and hashCode use all components for logical equality.
  • • Instances are immutable because components are final.
Limitation
Records cannot declare additional instance fields and cannot extend other classes; they are focused single-use data carriers.

screens.title: Records in practice: custom methods and immutability
screens.narratorSegment: Records are concise but not featureless. You may add custom methods, static fields, or compact constructors to validate components. However, you cannot add instance fields outside the declared components. A typical pattern is to provide derived or formatting helpers inside the record. For example, a Book record can include a getBookInfo method that returns a composed string of title, author, and year. Records remain immutable so any attempt to change a component after creation is a design error; the compiler and runtime semantics enforce immutability. When you need validation you can add a compact constructor that checks parameters and throws an exception if invalid. Using records makes your intent explicit: this type is a data carrier with stable state. A misconception is thinking records are identical to JavaBeans — they do not have setters and are intended for immutable use. Choose records when you want immutable value semantics and reduced boilerplate. Records in practice: custom methods and immutability means use records for immutable data with optional helper methods and validation via compact constructors.. In practical terms, add helpers while keeping data immutable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Record Details
Book record example
record Book(String title, String author, int yearPublished) {
  public String getBookInfo() {
    return title + " by " + author + " (" + yearPublished + ")";
  }

  // compact constructor for validation
  public Book {
    if (title == null || author == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing data");
  }
}
Records generate accessors like title() and author(). Attempting to change components after construction is not possible because components are final.
Key Takeaway

Records let you focus on data and behavior that derives directly from components, while preserving immutability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Hands-on: Currency & Transaction
Code template
import java.time.LocalDate;

public enum Currency {
    USD("$"),
    EUR("€"),
    GBP("£"),
    JPY("¥");

    private final String symbol;
    private Currency(String symbol) { this.symbol = symbol; }
    public String getSymbol() { return symbol; }
    public void displayCurrency() { System.out.println(this.name() + " (" + symbol + ")"); }
}

record Transaction(String description, double amount, Currency currencyType, java.time.LocalDate transactionDate) {
    public boolean isLargeTransaction() { return amount > 1000.0; }
}

// In main: iterate currencies and create Transaction instances
What to observe
  • • Currency constants each carry a symbol and provide displayCurrency for human-readable output.
  • • Transaction instances print with an auto-generated toString and compare by value using equals.
  • • Records remain immutable; there are no setters for transaction components.
  • • Trying to create a Currency from an arbitrary string would be an error; enums restrict choices at the type level.
Use this template as the basis for a small test harness to validate symbols, toString output, and equality behavior.

screens.title: Record vs POJO: trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Records are excellent for small, immutable value types where the primary purpose is storing data. They reduce boilerplate and provide correct equality semantics out of the box. However, records are not a universal replacement for classes. If your type requires mutable state, complex inheritance, or additional instance fields beyond the declared components, a regular class or a well-designed POJO is more appropriate. Records cannot extend other classes, which rules them out for some inheritance-based designs. Also, if you need observable setters, lifecycle hooks, or heavy identity semantics not based purely on components, prefer a class. A good rule of thumb: choose records for simple, predictable data aggregation such as DTOs, messages, or immutable domain values. Use POJOs when you need mutability, full control over initialization logic, or to participate in an inheritance hierarchy. Understanding these trade-offs helps you keep your codebase consistent and maintainable. Record vs POJO: trade-offs means use records when immutability and concise value semantics matter; use classes when you need mutable state or inheritance.. In practical terms, when to use records and when to prefer a full class. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.narratorSegment: Enums and records support clean domain modeling when used together. Enums represent closed choices in the domain model — roles, states, currency types — while records model value objects and messages passed between layers. For example, a transaction record holding a Currency enum ties the choice of currency directly to the transaction’s type system, reducing errors when formatting or converting amounts. screens.title: Common mistakes and quick checks
screens.narratorSegment: As you adopt enums and records, watch for a few recurring mistakes. First, declaring an enum constructor as public is incorrect; enum constructors are implicitly private and should not be public. Second, using enums for values that are not fixed or may change at runtime defeats their purpose; prefer configuration or classes in those cases. Third, treating records like mutable beans by expecting setters will lead to confusion — records are immutable and components are final. Fourth, attempting to add instance fields beyond declared components in a record is not allowed. To check your understanding, compile small examples: create an enum with a constructor and compile it, verify you cannot instantiate the enum externally, and create a record then attempt to mutate it to see the compiler or runtime behavior. These quick experiments reveal the language’s guarantees and help you internalize correct usage patterns. When in doubt, choose the structure that matches the intended mutability and domain constraints. In this lesson you will explore two language features that make Java code clearer and safer: enums and records. Enums give you a typed set of named constants that can carry fields, constructors, and methods so each constant can behave like a small object. Records, introduced as a standard feature in Java 16, let you declare immutable data carriers without boilerplate for constructors, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString. You will see practical examples: a traffic light enum with actions and durations, and a book record that shows how records auto-generate accessors and equality. As you learn, notice common pitfalls: using enums for values that change, or assuming records are mutable like POJOs. We’ll also practice by building a Currency enum and a Transaction record to illustrate how these features combine in a realistic application. By the end you will understand when an enum improves type safety and when a record reduces boilerplate, and you’ll be able to pick the right tool for representing fixed choices or simple immutable data.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify when an enum is the right representation for a fixed set of choices, and implement enums with fields, constructors, and methods to capture behavior and data per constant. You will also be able to declare Java records to create concise, immutable data classes that automatically supply constructors, accessors, and equality semantics, and you will understand the trade-offs between records and traditional POJOs. Each objective is practical: you will write an enum that stores metadata like symbols or durations, and you will write a record that serves as a transaction or data transfer object. Understanding these features reduces boilerplate, improves type safety, and leads to clearer designs in concurrent and domain-driven code. Finally, you will learn to spot common mistakes such as misusing enums for variable data or trying to mutate record components after construction.

These applied objectives focus on writing and testing code. You will implement an enum with a custom field and method, and instantiate and iterate its constants, which shows how each constant is a formed instance at runtime. You will also implement a record for a simple transaction data structure and verify that its accessor methods, equality, and toString behave as expected. Practice will include detecting two common mistakes: declaring enum constructors with incorrect access modifiers and attempting to modify record components after construction. Recognizing these errors early helps you avoid design issues: enums are for fixed sets and records are for immutable aggregation. This practical set of skills prepares you to refactor older code that used static final constants into safer enums, and to replace simple POJOs with records when immutability and concise declarations improve clarity.

Before enums, Java code commonly used public static final integers or strings to name fixed values. That pattern allows invalid assignments, loses semantic type information, and requires the reader to know the valid range by convention. An enum is a special class representing a fixed set of instances; it prevents invalid values at compile time because the type itself limits possible assignments. Enums also permit fields, methods, and constructors so each constant can bundle data and behavior. For example, if you model traffic lights, a plain integer gives you no direct place for the action text or duration. Using an enum you can store both and call methods like getDuration. A common misconception is that enums are only simple labels; in fact they are full-featured types and can implement interfaces, be used in switch statements, and be iterated. Use enums when the set of allowed values is closed and meaningful in the domain. When values are open-ended or configuration-driven, prefer classes or other structures. An enum declaration defines a special class whose constants are predefined instances. Each constant you list at the top is created by calling the enum’s constructor. Enum constructors are implicitly private, which prevents external code from creating new instances. You can add fields that all constants hold, initialize them via the constructor, and expose behavior through methods. For example the TrafficLightColor enum attaches an action string and duration in seconds to each color. Iterating over TrafficLightColor. values() returns every defined constant, and calling methods on each constant accesses its associated data. Remember three core ideas. First, an enum is a special class representing a closed set of named instances. Use it when the domain values are fixed and you want type safety and the ability to attach fields and methods to each constant. Second, a record is a concise way to declare immutable data carriers: the compiler provides a canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString. Prefer records for simple DTOs and value objects where immutability and minimal boilerplate are desired. Third, understand the trade-offs: records are not suitable for mutable or inheritance-heavy designs, and enums should not model values that change at runtime. Keep these three principles in mind when designing domain models, and validate your choices with small compile-and-run tests to observe the language guarantees in action. Keep a short mental checklist. First, enums: each constant is an instance; you can add fields, constructors and methods; enum constructors are not public. Second, records: declare components and get canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString for free; records are immutable and cannot add instance fields. Third, apply the right tool: choose enums when the set of values is closed and meaningful, choose records when you need immutable value semantics and minimal boilerplate. These three reminders help you make small but powerful design decisions quickly when modeling domain data or replacing legacy static constants.
